title: The Athenaeum — Nightly Sittings
subtitle: Drawn from that night's Nightly Discourse Report: every political, cultural, and religious story, each put to a table of historical thinkers.

briefing.question: When is impeachment the remedy for bad judgment rather than lawbreaking? Does a legislature that declines to use its war powers lose them?
briefing.agreed: Grave abuse of trust, not mere bad judgment, is impeachable; a Congress that will not judge weakens itself.
briefing.split: Hamilton, the record; Madison, use it or lose it; Aristotle, is it wise; Locke, the people judge.

briefing.question: Are the rules of a deliberative body a neutral inheritance to protect, or tools to set aside when the cause is urgent? What does a defeated party owe its voters: new faces or the same principles?
briefing.agreed: Rules that slow majorities protect every party in turn.
briefing.split: Madison, reform not suspend; Burke, principles over faces; Aristotle, easy change weakens law; Tocqueville, brakes.

briefing.question: Is private virtue a public matter for those who hold great power? Can a person be both a victim of deception and responsible for what it put at risk?
briefing.agreed: Great trust makes private conduct public; an inquiry is not proof.
briefing.split: Plato, self-rule; Aristotle, preventable ignorance answers; Juvenal, guard the inquiry; Washington, impartiality.

briefing.question: Is a republic of states or a nation of individuals the basic unit of American self-government? Can a constitution be changed by agreement rather than amendment?
briefing.agreed: A mixed national and federal system; both sides want every vote to count.
briefing.split: Madison, compacts are national business; Hamilton, breadth; Tocqueville, states as schools; Mill, equal votes, openly.

briefing.question: What do we owe the suffering of the past when we tell its story? Can art shock us toward truth, or does shock cheapen it?
briefing.agreed: Tell the past so victims stay human; threats are not criticism.
briefing.split: Aristotle, story not spectacle; Douglass, shock for humanity; Wiesel, memory; Plato, reason; Tolstoy, sincerity.

briefing.question: When does accountability become a mob? Is there a difference between punishing speech and declining to pay for it?
briefing.agreed: The joke was cruel, sponsors may leave, and accountability has limits.
briefing.split: Mill, withdraw but do not ruin; Aristotle, count the apology; Tocqueville, it reaches dissent; Smith, the fair spectator.

briefing.question: Should national memory be one shared symbol or many? Does remembering everyone risk honoring no one in particular?
briefing.agreed: Memory needs one common act; particular ones help if they gather under it.
briefing.split: Burke, ritual and platoons; Lincoln, a vow, not glory; Rousseau, one civic sentiment; Mill, one shared past.

briefing.question: What do people worship when they stop worshiping God? Can a call to personal holiness be heard from an institution still repairing its own failures?
briefing.agreed: Those who leave God still worship; holiness is heard from a Church facing its failures.
briefing.split: Augustine, disordered love; Aquinas, deeds; Pascal, the Church's idol; Kierkegaard, alone; Weber, conduct.

briefing.question: Is persuading someone to change their faith an act of love or an intrusion? Who protects the conscience: the state, the family, or the person alone?
briefing.agreed: Conversion by inducement is no conversion; intimidation is no answer.
briefing.split: Locke, ordinary law for fraud; Aquinas, teaching is charity; Gandhi, no proselytism, no mobs; Madison, conscience.

briefing.question: Can a public servant hold, and voice, a harsh judgment of a faith and still serve its believers justly? Where is the line between criticizing a belief and despising the believer?
briefing.agreed: Opinions are free, equal treatment is owed; conduct is the test.
briefing.split: Jefferson, conduct not creed; Mill, stigma; Ashoka, restraint; Brandeis, more speech; Aristotle, common good.

briefing.question: Can a nation keep an established church and still treat all faiths as equal citizens? What does a church owe the state, and the state the church?
briefing.agreed: No one shut out of civil life for faith; face change openly.
briefing.split: Hooker, the old identity is gone; Burke, deliberate change; Locke, the mixing; Williams, end it; Madison, principle.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Hamilton speaks first because the report names his Federalist No. 65 on impeachment as the abuse of a public trust, and he wrote most directly on what the remedy reaches and how faction distorts it. Madison follows because the report cites his view that the executive is the branch most prone to war, and because he wrote most on each branch guarding its own powers. Aristotle is seated because the report names his practical wisdom, which asks whether a remedy fits the moment as well as whether it is permitted, and because his account of equity explains why written law never covers every case. Locke closes because his chapter on prerogative asks what happens when the executive acts beyond the law, and who judges it afterward. Cicero and Aquinas, seated last night on the war itself, are left off because tonight's question is the remedy and the legislature's own duty, not whether the war is just. The congressman, the Secretary, the Senate leader, and other officials named in the report are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: when is impeachment the remedy for bad judgment rather than lawbreaking, and does a legislature that declines to use its war powers lose them? The report gives one side as supporters of impeachment, who say the war ran far past the War Powers Resolution's sixty-day limit without authorization from Congress, and that a Congress that will not even vote on it has given up its most basic check. The other side is most Republicans, including some frustrated with the war, who say disagreement over a war's conduct is not a high crime or misdemeanor, that the effort is a partisan removal campaign led by a defeated lame-duck member, and that the strikes crippled Iran's nuclear and naval capacity. Hamilton, the report begins with your paper on impeachment. You speak first.

turn.text: I did not confine impeachment to crimes in a statute book. I wrote that its subjects are “The subjects of its jurisdiction are those offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust.” (Federalist No. 65) And I added: “They are of a nature which may with peculiar propriety be denominated POLITICAL, as they relate chiefly to injuries done immediately to the society itself.” (Federalist No. 65) So the supporters of these articles stand on my text when they say the remedy can reach a grave misuse of office that no criminal code names. Bad judgment alone is not a high crime; bad judgment that disregards the limits of the office, such as making war without the authority the Constitution places elsewhere, can be.

It is a judgment that this House, in this season, will not hear the case. chairs.modern_read: Hamilton held that impeachment reaches serious abuses of public trust, not only statutory crimes, so making war without proper authority could qualify where ordinary bad judgment would not. But he warned that impeachment votes tend to follow party strength, and he would want the case judged on the record of authorization rather than the war's results.

turn.text: Hamilton has stated the remedy. I would turn the question around, because the report asks whether a legislature that declines its war power loses it. I wrote to Jefferson that the Constitution supposes what history shows, that the executive is the branch most interested in war and most prone to it, and so it vested the question of war in the legislature with studied care (letter to Jefferson, 1798, paraphrased). We built the separation on a warning: “The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.” (Federalist No. 47)

setup.text: After three closed-door meetings, Senate Republicans re-elected their leader by acclamation, having first voted 31 to 15 to proceed rather than delay, and kept the rest of the leadership team. Democrats are on track for 54 Senate seats and about 255 House seats in January, and some conservatives faulted the leader for refusing to break the filibuster to pass a voter-identification bill.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Madison speaks first because the report names his Federalist No. 10 and No. 51 on institutions that slow majorities, and he wrote most on why a republic should restrain even its own majority. Burke follows because the report names his case for prudent continuity, set against the reformer's warning that institutions that never change after failure stop serving, and his writings on party speak to what a defeated party owes. Aristotle is seated because his Politics weighs the cost of changing laws lightly and describes citizens ruling and being ruled in turn, which is the minority's position in January. Tocqueville closes because he wrote the classic account of the tyranny of the majority and of its limits. The playwright Robert Bolt, whose scene with Thomas More the report cites, is left off as a twentieth-century dramatist in copyright and because the lines are his stage character's, not More's own writing. The senators and commentators named in the report are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: are the rules of a deliberative body a neutral inheritance to protect, or tools to set aside when the cause is urgent, and what does a defeated party owe its voters: new faces or the same principles? The report gives one side as the leader's defenders, who say the losses were about affordability, not Senate procedure, that the filibuster he protected will now shield Republican priorities in the minority, and that a steady, well-liked leader is what a shrunken conference needs. The other side is critics on the right, who say leadership squandered two years of majority power by refusing to override the filibuster on election integrity, judges, and the President's orders, and that re-electing the same leaders after a wipeout means no one learned anything. Madison, the report cites your papers on majorities. Begin.

chairs.name: James Madison

turn.text: We wrote the Constitution against a complaint I recorded plainly: that in the states “measures are too often decided, not according to the rules of justice and the rights of the minor party, but by the superior force of an interested and overbearing majority.” (Federalist No. 10) The Senate was meant to slow a passing majority, and the filibuster is not in our text, but it serves the same purpose by habit. The defenders are right that a rule protecting the minority is valuable precisely because every party will be the minority someday, and this conference will be in January.

turn.text: Yet I did not think rules sacred in themselves. They serve the deeper design: “you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself.” (Federalist No. 51) A rule that keeps the government from controlling itself is good; a rule that keeps it from governing at all, when the people have spoken repeatedly, may need reform by deliberate and general change, not by a majority suspending it for one bill it favors. The critics' urgency about voter identification may be sincere, but a rule broken for an urgent cause is broken for every cause that follows.

That is the defenders' case, and I think it a sound one.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: what do we owe the suffering of the past when we tell its story, and can art shock us toward truth, or does shock cheapen it? turn.text: Aristotle wants the shock earned by the story. I knew slavery from the inside, and I can tell you that polite argument did not move the nation. Augustine, the report begins with your Confessions.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Jefferson speaks first because the report names his Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, which separates a person's religious opinions from his civil standing, and the report notes it cuts both ways here. Mill follows because the report names his harm principle, and his On Liberty also warns against stigmatizing those who disagree. Ashoka is seated because his Rock Edict XII is one of the oldest public commands on restraint of speech about other faiths, given by a ruler to his officials. Brandeis is seated because the report names his rule of more speech, not enforced silence; his Whitney concurrence is a U.S. judicial opinion in the public domain. Aristotle closes because the report names his idea that rulers must serve the common good of all the governed. Washington's Newport letter, seated on related questions recently, is left off to keep the table at five. The board member and the speakers are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: can a public servant hold, and voice, a harsh judgment of a faith and still serve its believers justly, and where is the line between criticizing a belief and despising the believer? The report gives one side as critics, including Muslim families, who say an elected official who calls a world religion a cult has shown he cannot serve all the students in his district, that words from public officials lend license to harassment, and that he should resign. The other side is the member's supporters, who say he has a First Amendment right to share political views on his own page, that criticizing a religion's ideas is not the same as attacking its followers, and that public officials should not be pushed out for opinions voters can judge at the ballot box. Jefferson, the report says your statute cuts both ways.
